place.zh: 沂中医 · 学生健身房 · 国庆
place.en: Yizhong · the student gym · National Day week

setup.zh: 国庆，一个人憋着气卧推，四十公斤的杠落在胸口上。阿禾教他：绷住，推，吐。试训末一名替补。
setup.en: National Day week: benching alone, breath held, forty kilos came down on his chest. Ahe teaches him: brace, push, breathe out. He makes the team as the last substitute.

recap.zh: 憋气卧推，杠落在胸口；「绷住，推，吐」；替补第三，末一个进队。
recap.en: Breath held on the bench, the bar on his chest; "brace, push, breathe out"; third substitute, the last one in.

en: Forty kilos, down on his chest.
Third substitute, the last one in.

story.zh:
国庆第五天下午，沈芒一个人躺在学生健身房的卧推凳上，憋着一口气，眼前一黑，四十公斤的杠铃落了下来。

黑里头一张小板凳，他太奶坐在上头，老花镜往下一拉，这回没招手，也没说饺子：「芒啊。喘气。」

杠落在胸口上。要是再往上偏一点，就是脖子。

这事，得往回倒五天。

十月一日早上七点半，健身房里一个人也没有。他躺上卧推凳，握住那根杠——杠是温的。这屋子朝北，不是太阳晒的，是手捂的。

「我的。」镜子那头，马小宝拿毛巾擦着脖子转过身来，「刚推完。一百公斤，五个。」

沈芒把阿禾那张通知背给他听：十月十七试训，三项过两项进替补；力量那一项，卧推四十公斤，连推五个。他今天能推三十，三个。

「差十公斤、两个。小意思。」马小宝下巴一扬，拿鼻孔对着他道，「天天练，练到推不动为止。推的时候憋住气，一口气推上去。漏了气，力就散了。」

那张健身卡是中秋夜里办的，一学期三百：两百是回家的车票钱，一百是他妈的过节钱。他跟家里说，国庆学校有集训。

第二天他去古籍部，问葛奶奶有没有《易筋经》那种，天生没力气的人也练得出来的。葛奶奶从老花镜上头看他：「易筋经没有。倒有一句硬话，葛洪的书里抄过一句更老的：『我命在我不在天。』」临走取包，她还在絮叨插队那会儿的搬运站，顺嘴一句：「……扛大包的都喊号子。号子不是唱给人听的，是叫人一使劲，就出气。」

他蹲在门边，又抽出那本薄薄的手札，翻到一页：「吐长于吸，心自缓。心缓，手乃稳。」页边一行铅笔小字，又小又急：「试之。吐长于纳，心果缓。」

那句硬话，他像吞了一块热炭；号子和手札，他都没往心里去。

国庆七天，六一七只剩他一个。第四张空床上，他的泡面箱又摞了两箱——钱叫卡吃了，剩下的撑到十一月一号，只够吃泡面。他妈视频里眯着眼瞅：「你手里端的什么？」他把碗挪出镜头：「夜宵。食堂饭吃完了。」

第五天北风刮了一夜，他抱被子上天台去晒，往西北望，天边横着一道青灰的山脊，淡得像拿铅笔描的。宿管阿姨拍着被子道：「蒙山。一年没几回看得见。」他是德州平原上长大的，看着看着，心里有一块地方静了一静。

下午他给自己加到了四十。推了五天，三十还是三个——命在我，那就是练得还不够狠。

他是叫杠压醒的。拿脚蹬着地，把杠一点一点往肚子上滚，滚到大腿根，才坐起来。

玻璃门一响，马小宝拎着摇杯进来，站住了，脸上的笑没了。他一只手把杠提回架子上，像放一根晾衣杆：「憋气是我教的，我没教你一个人憋！」掏出手机，「领队，健身房，新队员自杀！」

阿禾十分钟就到了，白大褂没脱，马尾辫跑散了。她叫他躺平，腿搭上凳子，看他的眼睛，按他胸口那道红印。

「憋着气硬推，胸口里的压力顶上去，回心的血过不来，脑子先断了供。」她拔了笔帽又按上，「落在脖子上，你现在不是坐在这儿听我说话。」

她拿指头往他肚子上一戳，他「哎」一声，肚子一紧。「深吸一口，绷住，是对的。绷住，推，吐——不是憋着跟它耗。」

半个钟头以后，她把片卸到三十，站在他头顶上虚托着杠。吸，绷住，推——「呵——」。一个，两个，三个，四个，第五个晃了晃，到底上去了。

三十公斤，五个。他想起葛奶奶那句号子。

「你平时吃什么？」阿禾问。

他想起空床上那三箱泡面，想起她本子上要是添上三个字「吃不起」——

「食堂。」

她看了他一会儿，「嗯」了一声，记下了。又问：「你为什么来打球？」

他盯着天花板上的灯管：「……想跑快一点。」

十月十六日，试训前一天，阿禾在器材室给他称：五十八点九公斤，比九月还轻。「长的那点力气，是脑子学会了一齐使劲。肉，一两没长。」

「我天生就这身板。人家天生一米九三。」

她在那一行底下添了一行，转过来给他看：「天生的定上限；离上限多远，是练的。」又问：「你吃的什么，再说一遍。」

「……食堂。」

第二天试训，二十米往返跑，二十三个人里第十四；罚球十个进三个，正卡在线上；卧推四十，第五个推到一半停住了。他没憋——他记着那张小板凳。马小宝把杠接走，冲全场宣布：「咱们队的吉祥物，尽力了。」半个馆哄地笑了。

替补第三，末一个进队的。雷老师把表一合：「上个月，一千米倒数第一。没什么好笑的。」马小宝走过来拍他的肩，压低了嗓子：「过了两项。那句话，我先替你留着。」
story.en:
On the afternoon of the fifth day of the National Day holiday, Shen Mang lay alone on a bench in the student gym, holding his breath; his sight went black, and the forty-kilo barbell came down.

In the black was a little stool, his great-grandma sitting on it. She pulled her reading glasses down; this time she didn't wave, and she didn't mention dumplings: "Mang. Breathe."

The bar landed on his chest. A little higher, and it would have been his neck.

For this, we have to go back five days.

October the first, seven-thirty in the morning, and there was no one in the gym. He lay down on the bench and gripped the bar — the bar was warm. The room faced north; it wasn't the sun that had warmed it, it was hands.

"Mine." At the far end by the mirror Ma Xiaobao turned round, wiping his neck with a towel. "Just finished. A hundred kilos, five reps."

Shen Mang recited Ahe's notice to him: tryouts October seventeenth, pass two of three tests to make the reserves; the strength test was a forty-kilo bench press, five reps in a row. Today he could press thirty, three reps.

"Ten kilos and two reps short. Small stuff," said Ma Xiaobao, tipping his chin up to look at him down his nostrils. "Train every day, train till you can't press any more. When you press, hold your breath and push it up in one go. Let the air out and the power scatters."

He had bought the gym card on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, three hundred for the semester: two hundred was his train fare home, one hundred was his mom's holiday money. He told his family the school had team training over National Day.

The next day he went to the rare-books section and asked Granny Ge whether there was something like the *Yijin Jing*, something a person born without strength could still train with. Granny Ge looked at him over her reading glasses: "No *Yijin Jing*. But there's one hard saying — Ge Hong copied an older one into his book: 'My fate lies with me, not with Heaven.'" When he came to collect his bag on the way out, she was still rambling on about the freight depot back when she was sent down to the countryside, and added in passing: "...The men carrying sacks all chanted. The chant isn't sung for anyone to hear; it makes you breathe out the moment you heave."

Crouched by the door, he drew out that thin book of notes again and turned to a page: "Out longer than in, and the heart slows of itself. The heart slow, the hand is steady." In the margin a line of small pencil, small and hurried: "Tried it. Out longer than in — the heart did slow."

The hard saying he swallowed like a hot coal; the chant and the notes he didn't take to heart.

For the seven days of National Day, Room 617 had only him. On the fourth, empty bed his instant-noodle boxes were stacked two more high — the card had eaten his money, and what was left, to last till November the first, would only buy instant noodles. On video his mom squinted: "What's that you're holding?" He moved the bowl out of frame: "Late-night snack. The canteen food was finished."

On the fifth day the north wind blew all night. He carried his quilt up to the roof to air it, looked northwest, and on the horizon lay a blue-grey ridge, faint as if traced in pencil. The dorm auntie, beating a quilt, said, "Mount Meng. You don't see it many times a year." He had grown up on the Dezhou plain; looking and looking, some place in his heart went still for a moment.

In the afternoon he went up to forty. Five days of pressing, and thirty was still three reps — if fate lay with him, then he just hadn't trained hard enough.

It was the bar pressing on him that woke him. Pushing with his feet against the floor, he rolled the bar little by little down onto his stomach, down to the tops of his thighs, before he could sit up.

The glass door rattled; Ma Xiaobao came in carrying his shaker, stopped, and the smile went from his face. With one hand he lifted the bar back onto the rack like a clothes-drying pole: "I taught you to hold your breath, I didn't teach you to hold it on your own!" He pulled out his phone. "Manager, gym, new player suicide!"

Ahe was there in ten minutes, still in her white coat, her ponytail come loose from running. She had him lie flat with his legs up on the bench, looked into his eyes, pressed the red mark across his chest.

"Hold your breath and force it, the pressure in your chest goes up, the blood coming back to the heart can't get through, and the brain is the first to lose supply." She pulled off her pen cap and pushed it back on. "If it had come down on your neck, you wouldn't be sitting here listening to me."

She jabbed a finger into his stomach; he went "Ah" and his stomach tensed. "Take a deep breath, brace — that's right. Brace, press, breathe out — not hold your breath and grind it out."

Half an hour later she took the plates down to thirty and stood over his head, hands hovering under the bar. Breathe in, brace, press — "Haaa —". One, two, three, four; the fifth wobbled, and went up after all.

Thirty kilos, five reps. He thought of Granny Ge and the chant.

"What do you usually eat?" Ahe asked.

He thought of the three boxes of instant noodles on the empty bed, thought of her adding to her notebook the words "can't afford food" —

"The canteen."

She looked at him for a while, said "Mm," and wrote it down. Then she asked, "Why did you come to play ball?"

He stared at the tube light on the ceiling: "...I want to run a bit faster."

October the sixteenth, the day before tryouts, Ahe weighed him in the equipment room: fifty-eight point nine kilos, lighter than in September. "The bit of strength you've gained is your brain learning to make everything push together. Muscle, you haven't put on an ounce."

"I was born with this build. Other people are born six foot four."

She added a line under that row and turned it round to show him: "What you're born with sets the ceiling; how far you are from it is training." Then she asked, "What do you eat? Tell me again."

"...The canteen."

The next day at tryouts: twenty-metre shuttle run, fourteenth of twenty-three; free throws, three of ten, right on the line; bench press forty, the fifth rep stopped halfway up. He didn't hold his breath — he remembered the little stool. Ma Xiaobao took the bar off him and announced to the whole gym: "Our team mascot. He gave it his all." Half the gym burst out laughing.

Third reserve, the last one onto the team. Coach Lei snapped his watch shut: "Last month, dead last in the thousand metres. Nothing funny about it." Ma Xiaobao came over and patted his shoulder, voice low: "Passed two. That thing I'm going to say for you — I'll hang on to it for now."

exits.means: goes on to the team scrimmage
